article_text:
A24 ’s The Invite has been tapped to receive the Palm Springs International Film Awards’ Vanguard Award, the first of a string of honors that will be announced as part of the 2027 Palm Springs Film Festival ‘s opening-night gala January 7.

The film’s director-star Olivia Wilde and her co-stars Seth Rogen, Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton are slated to attend the gala, which annually kicks off the festival in the SoCal desert. The Vanguard Award is given in recognition of a director and cast’s collective work on an exceptional film project, with past recipients including Hamnet last year as well Green Book and The Shape of Water before they went on to with the Best Picture Oscar .

Related Stories

‘The Invite’ Review: Director & Star Olivia Wilde Navigates Dinner Parties, Monogamy & Orgies In Whip-Smart Marital Comedy — Sundance Film Festival

How Indie Comedy ‘The Invite’ Crashed The Summer Blockbuster Party; Is The Next Stop Broadway?

The Invite centers on dinner party between two neighboring couples spirals into an unpredictable evening of revelations and desire, revealing the hilarity and humanity in the complexities of marriage, intimacy and relationships.

Watch on Deadline

The pic hit theaters in late June becoming one of the year’s top-grossing limited debuts. It has grossed $61.2 million to become an indie summer hit both domestically and overseas.

“With The Invite , Olivia Wilde has made a film that is both comedic and deeply human. In addition to directing, she stars alongside three of the most compelling actors working today: Seth Rogen, Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton,” said festival chairman Nachhattar Singh Chandi. “Each of them brings something irreplaceable to this story, and together they’ve created something that has stayed with audiences long after the credits roll. We are thrilled to honor this incredible team with this year’s Vanguard Award.”

The Invite premiered this year at Sundance and earlier in the week picked up a co-leading four nominations at the Gotham Film Awards including for Will McCormack and Rashida Jones’ adapted screenplay.

The Palm Springs Film Festival runs January 7-18, 2027.

Weekly Newsletter

Diaries of a Primitive Man

John Yau on Roy Lichtenstein, Megan O’Grady on John Berger, and Paddy Johnson answers the question: Do I need an agent?

Hyperallergic )

It’s a sunny October afternoon in Manhattan and the steps of the Metropolitan Museum of Art are bustling with visitors. Tourists pose for selfies against the museum’s facade; street vendors sell chopped-up hotdogs in a nest of French fries; and the sound of saxophone music drowns into the symphony of splashing water fountains and honking cars on Fifth Avenue. So many types of people; the only ones missing are the Lenape whose land was stolen so we could enjoy this fine Indigenous Peoples’ Day on the steps of The Met.

Inside the museum, a blockbuster exhibition about Abstract Expressionist painters Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock is jam-packed. The show is as much about their mutual influence as it is about their marriage, their most difficult collaboration.

I hear a woman from behind accusing me of “White privilege” because I apparently cut her in line. I turn around and say, “What White privilege? Look at me.” She takes a quick look and corrects herself, “Okay, so male privilege.”

I turn on Democracy Now and listen to a 30-minute conversation about settler colonialism. I notice a Jeep Wrangler ahead of me with a sticker proudly announcing, “primitive man.” I shudder at first but quickly come to admire the driver’s honesty. War Secretary Pete Hegseth threatens to livestream an execution by firing squad.

At the Brooklyn Museum, I pause by a display of Indigenous Kachina dolls that were given to Hopi girls and women living in what is now Arizona. Who made them and how they got here we don’t exactly know, but now they belong to the museum’s Center for Feminist Art.

At the end of the day, my shoulders are tense and my brain cooked, and my only wish is to lie down idea-free, opinionless, primitive.

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

Roy Lichtenstein Has Lost His Luster

Roy Lichtenstein’s paintings stick in your mind. They are memorable and congenial. When I went to Roy Lichtenstein: Like New, the first major survey of his work in more than 30 years, at the Whitney Museum, I expected to be surprised by something new the curators dug up in their research into the sources of many of the more than 130 paintings, sculptures, drawings, and prints on view. I was not initially disappointed. | John Yau

editorial_excerpt_zh: 让·皮埃尔和埃利安·拉丰（Jean-Pierre and Éliane Laffont）：定格历史，编辑记忆。总有一些人拍摄他们所处的时代，也有一些人在岁月的流转中…… […] Cet article The Questionnaire : Jean-Pierre & Éliane Laffont by Carole Schmitz est apparu en premier sur The Eye of…

"总有一些人拍摄他们所处的时代，也有一些人在岁月的流转中最终成为了它的档案保管员。让·皮埃尔·拉丰（Jean-Pierre Laffont）兼具这两种身份。自1960年代以来，他一直以极其敏锐的目光注视着美国——它的反叛、它的断裂、它的梦想、它的无名之辈和公众人物，并带着一种局外人特有的距离感；尽管身为外国人，他最终却对所拍摄的国家有了深入骨髓的了解与其说他的作品是一组影像的集合，不如说是一部浩瀚的美国编年史，其中充满了暴力、自由、抗议，以及最核心的那些具象化这些时代的形形色色的人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但一张照片不会在快门关闭的那一刻结束。人们还得审视它、挑选它、将它与其他照片并置，并理解它在今天所传达的信息——这些信息在昨天或许并未被表达出来。正是在这里，埃利安·拉丰（Éliane "你在人脸、风景或物体中寻找什么细节？JPL：我从未拍摄过风景、日落或物体。每个人都是上镜的，或者说世上只有糟糕的摄影师。EL：在照片中吸引我的不是细节，而是它唤起的记忆以及带给我的情感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在你看来，在摄影中技巧有时会凌驾于情感之上吗？JPL：当然会，对于那些把摄影当成艺术的人来说是这样。我不这么看。EL：是的，很遗憾。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "自从社交媒体兴起以来，有什么改变了？JPL：糟糕的构图、愚蠢的题材——简而言之，那些算不上真正的照片。EL：像我这样糟糕的摄影师也可以发布日常生活中迷人的照片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你绝对推荐的一个 Instagram 账号？JPL：不知道。EL：我喜欢我的摄影记者朋友们的 Instagram 账号。", Jean-Pierre Laffont belongs to both categories. Since the 1960s, he has looked very closely at America, its revolts, its fractures, its dreams, its anonymous figures and its public personalities , with the particular distance of someone who, although a foreigner, ultimately came to know intimately the country he was photographing. His work is less a collection of images than a vast American chronicle, marked by violence, freedom, protest and, above all, by the people who embody them."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But a photograph does not end when the shutter closes. It still has to be looked at, selected, placed alongside others, and understood for what it says today that it may not have said yesterday. This is where Éliane Laffont comes in. Editor, art director, curator and an essential figure in the history of major photojournalism agencies, she has devoted much of her life to this work, as decisive as it is often invisible: looking at other people’s images and recognizing, sometimes before anyone else, which ones deserve to endure. Between them, then, there is more than a love story and more than a story about photography. There is a dialogue between two ways of seeing: one that goes out to encounter reality, and another that returns to the images to give them a second life. Jean-Pierre photographs in the urgency of the present; Éliane works within the longer time of editing, memory and storytelling."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Their current work makes this particularly clear. Rebels with a Cause , their new book, brings together Jean-Pierre’s photographs of American protest movements from the 1960s to the 1980s: civil rights, Vietnam, Black Power, feminism, counterculture and the LGBTQ+ movement, while offering, through Éliane’s eye, a new way of looking at these archives. In Paris this November, an exhibition and a sale of more than 150 prints extend this rediscovery."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "More than fifty years later, these images are strangely unsettling: they speak of an America that seems to belong to History and, at the same time, of a present that sometimes resembles it dangerously. article_text:
Jean-Pierre and Éliane Laffont : Photographing History, editing memory

There are those who photograph their time, and those who, with the passing of years, eventually become its archivists. Jean-Pierre Laffont belongs to both categories. Since the 1960s, he has looked very closely at America, its revolts, its fractures, its dreams, its anonymous figures and its public personalities , with the particular distance of someone who, although a foreigner, ultimately came to know intimately the country he was photographing. His work is less a collection of images than a vast American chronicle, marked by violence, freedom, protest and, above all, by the people who embody them.

But a photograph does not end when the shutter closes. It still has to be looked at, selected, placed alongside others, and understood for what it says today that it may not have said yesterday. This is where Éliane Laffont comes in. Editor, art director, curator and an essential figure in the history of major photojournalism agencies, she has devoted much of her life to this work, as decisive as it is often invisible: looking at other people’s images and recognizing, sometimes before anyone else, which ones deserve to endure. Between them, then, there is more than a love story and more than a story about photography. There is a dialogue between two ways of seeing: one that goes out to encounter reality, and another that returns to the images to give them a second life. Jean-Pierre photographs in the urgency of the present; Éliane works within the longer time of editing, memory and storytelling.

Their current work makes this particularly clear. Rebels with a Cause , their new book, brings together Jean-Pierre’s photographs of American protest movements from the 1960s to the 1980s: civil rights, Vietnam, Black Power, feminism, counterculture and the LGBTQ+ movement, while offering, through Éliane’s eye, a new way of looking at these archives. In Paris this November, an exhibition and a sale of more than 150 prints extend this rediscovery.

More than fifty years later, these images are strangely unsettling: they speak of an America that seems to belong to History and, at the same time, of a present that sometimes resembles it dangerously. So, what remains when the present becomes an archive? What does someone who has spent a lifetime looking still see? And what does the woman who has spent her life looking at other people’s images recognize? It is in this space, between lived time and observed time, that this Questionnaire begins.

Instagram : @elianelaffont – @jplaffont

Current affairs

Rebels with a Cause by Jean-Pierre & Éliane Laffont, published by Damiani, 192 pages, in English.

Éliane and Jean-Pierre Laffont will be at the Grand Palais for Paris Photo for a book signing at the Damiani booth, L03, on Friday, November 13, from 6:00 p.m.

On Monday, November 16, Gros & Delettrez is devoting an entire sale to Jean-Pierre Laffont, one of the great witnesses to America from the 1960s to the 1980s. More than 150 prints compose the portrait of a country in turmoil: from civil rights marches to protests against the Vietnam War, from Black Power to the fall of Richard Nixon. An America captured at close range — in the streets, in the crowds, and in those moments of upheaval when History ceases to be abstract and takes on human faces.

Your first photographic trigger? Éliane Laffont: Jean-Pierre was the person who introduced me to photography.

A photographic memory from your childhood? Jean-Pierre Laffont: Cartier-Bresson’s books The Europeans , The Decisive Moment , and The Family of Man . Éliane Laffont: No photographic memories. I come from a family of intellectuals for whom only words mattered.

The camera of your childhood? JPL: A Kodak box camera, 6×9. EL: No camera. We didn’t even have a television.

The camera you use today? JPL: Leica and Sony. EL: A Leica given to me by ICP when I won the award for best book on the Gulf War.

The man or woman of photography who inspired you? JPL: Cartier-Bresson, Ernst Haas, Weegee, Lewis Hine. EL: Jean-Pierre Laffont, Raymond Depardon, Mary Ellen Mark, Dorothea Lange, Eugene Richards.

The photograph you wish you had taken? JPL: Cartier-Bresson’s photograph of the Indian women waiting for the monsoon. EL: André Kertész’s photograph on the cover of his book On Reading .

The one that moved you the most? JPL: The naked Vietnamese girl running after being burned by napalm, photographed by Nick Ut. EL: The naked Vietnamese girl running after being burned by napalm, photographed by Nick Ut.

And the one that made you angry? JPL: Recent photographs manipulated by artificial intelligence. EL: All photographs transformed by artificial intelligence.

Which photograph changed the world? JPL: Eddie Adams’s photograph of the execution of a Viet Cong prisoner by a Vietnamese police officer. This photograph probably helped bring the Vietnam War to an end. EL: Jean-Pierre’s photograph showing children working in garbage dumps in India.

And which photograph changed your world? JPL: Underwater photographs in general fascinate me. EL: Brent Stirton’s photograph of a gorilla killed at Bukima in the Congo. And all of Donna Ferrato’s photographs about violence against women, Living With the Enemy .

A key image in your personal pantheon? JPL: I don’t remember the photographs I took, only the ones I wasn’t able to take. EL: All the photographs of my family.

What interests you most in an image? JPL: Its composition, clarity, honesty and power, because then I will never forget the photograph. EL: The emotions it evokes.

What details do you look for in a face, a landscape or an object? JPL: I have never photographed landscapes, sunsets or objects. Everyone is photogenic, or there are simply bad photographers. EL: It is not details that interest me in a photograph, but the memories it evokes and the emotions it brings me.

Elliott Erwitt said: “Color is descriptive. Black and white is interpretive.” Do you agree? JPL: No, I don’t agree. I only see in color, and if I worked in black and white, it was because there was no other film available, or because clients didn’t want color. EL: I agree with Elliott. Black and white expresses a personal vision that provokes a great deal of emotion and reflection in me.

In your opinion, can technique sometimes take precedence over emotion in photography? JPL: Certainly, for those who consider photography an art. That’s not how I see it EL: Yes, unfortunately.

Is beauty in photography, for you, purely aesthetic? JPL: No. My documents are often poignant, and aesthetics have no place in them. I am a photojournalist. I bear witness. EL: No. Beauty can be extraordinarily moving, especially when it is not purely aesthetic.

What elements can make silence visible in a photograph? JPL: I am not sensitive to noise, nor even to music. EL: I am more sensitive to noise and fury in a photograph.

Does the uniqueness of a photograph come from the moment or from staging? Can a photograph be truer than reality? JPL: If it is truer than reality, then it has succeeded and does not need a caption. EL: Photographs become iconic when they become a metaphor for reality, making them truer than reality and therefore unforgettable.

Can a photograph change our perception of an event? JPL: Yes. I have often photographed precious, poignant moments that are rare testimonies. EL: Yes. It happens to me every day that a photograph changes my perception of an event and makes me want to act.

Is photography a testimony or a form of manipulation? JPL: For me, I want to be a witness to my time. That is what I have always done with my camera. EL: Photography is the most magnificent form of testimony there is.

What makes a good photograph? JPL: One that does not need a caption, one that says everything in that frozen instant. EL: A photograph that makes you discover, feel and remember.

In your opinion, what quality is necessary to be a good photographer? JPL: Knowing how to compose instantly and knowing where to position yourself in front of an event. EL: Being in the right place at the right time, remaining invisible in order to capture it properly, working every day, staying informed and remaining humble.

How do you choose your projects? JPL: With passion, and with a great deal of research. I spend a lot of time on them. EL: Read everything, see everything, take an interest in the world and in people, and want to bear witness.

How would you describe your creative process? JPL: When I begin a reportage, I have a visual emotion, but very quickly it turns into visual erosion and I no longer see my subject. It is inside my camera and I have to move on to something else. EL: Wanting to want something every morning when I wake up.

An upcoming project that is particularly close to your heart? JPL: I am 92 years old and unfortunately I can no longer run around as much as I would like. EL: Making photography books is my passion.

The person you would like to photograph? JPL: No one in particular comes to mind. EL: I prefer to look.

The person by whom you would like to be photographed? JPL: No. I don’t have that ego. EL: Helmut Newton took a photograph of me that I love. I would also have liked to have been photographed by Richard Avedon.

An indispensable photography book? JPL: The Family of Man. EL: I have a library of nearly 400 photography books. They are all indispensable to me.

What is the last photograph you took? JPL: I don’t remember the photographs I have taken. EL: I am not a photographer, but I think I take very nice photographs of my granddaughters.

On social media, are you more Instagram, Facebook or TikTok, and why? JPL: Instagram. It is run by my wife, Éliane. EL: I really like Instagram. It allows me to stay connected with my friends around the world.

What has changed since the rise of social media? JPL: Bad compositions, stupid subjects in short, photographs that aren’t really photographs. EL: Even a bad photographer like me can post charming photographs of everyday life.

One Instagram account you absolutely recommend? JPL: No idea. EL: I like the Instagram accounts of my photojournalist friends.

What is your view of AI? JPL: I want to follow with passion, as best I can, the improvements AI might bring to old, damaged or faded photographs. EL: It fascinates me and worries me.

Color or black and white? JPL: Color. EL: Black and white.

Natural light or artificial light? JPL: As a young photographer, I loved working in the studio and mixing different kinds of light. EL: Natural light, and also artificial light that resembles natural light.

Which city do you find the most photogenic? JPL: Varanasi, India. EL: It all depends on the photographer.

The city, country or culture you dream of discovering? JPL: I must have spent two years in India over several trips. This country still makes me dream. EL: Every journey is a discovery.

The place you never tire of? JPL: India, Nepal, South Korea. EL: New York.

The image that, for you, represents the current state of the world? JPL: The front page of your favorite newspaper tomorrow morning. EL: Edvard Munch’s The Scream in black and white — not a photograph, but it could be one.

In your opinion, what is missing from today’s world? JPL: Honesty and impartiality. EL: Love for others.

If God existed, would you ask him to pose for you, or would you take a selfie with him? JPL: Since I have always doubted Him, I would be happy to photograph Him and prove that I was wrong. EL: A selfie with Him, to make sure every morning that He is on my side.

Your favorite drug? JPL: Television. EL: My work as a photo editor.

Your best way to disconnect? JPL: A good film. EL: Looking through a good photography book.

Your latest extravagance? JPL: A pressure cooker. EL: Having my favorite photographs printed in large format and hanging them on the wall.

Your greatest professional extravagance? JPL: Difficult question, because I have been lucky enough to get many scoops. If you don’t have luck, you cannot be a photojournalist. EL: Taking over Jean-Pierre’s photographic career and editing two million of his photographs.

The profession you would never have wanted to do? JPL: My parents’ profession: gynecology and obstetrics. EL: Accountant.

Which question throws you off the most? JPL: “What is your favorite photograph?” EL: “What is your favorite photograph?”

The last thing you did for the first time? JPL: I have done so many things for the first time that I don’t remember. EL: Every morning is a first time.

Your greatest regret? JPL: The images I was unable to make for all sorts of reasons, and the negatives and slides lost by my agencies. EL: My father wanted me to become a philosopher. I wish I had convinced him that what I do is just as important.

If you had to start all over again? JPL: It would be with a digital camera that calculates my white balance, tells me where I am, gives me the date and time… A dream for an old photographer. EL: Perhaps a writer, because I love words as much as photographs.

If I could organize your ideal dinner, who would be sitting around the table? JPL: I would rather have dinner alone with my wife, Éliane. EL: My whole family and my five favorite girlfriends.

What would you like people to say about you… afterwards? JPL: He never knew boredom… and now he’s going to get acquainted with it… EL: She had a fabulous life and no regrets.

The one thing people absolutely need to know about you? JPL: My sincerity. EL: My energy.

One last word? JPL: Thank you. EL: See you very soon — and let’s have a drink.

article_text:
Russell Brand , who was convicted of rape last week in London, posted on X Wednesday that his Instagram account has been removed by Meta.

Brand posted a screenshot reading, “We disabled your account. Our technology found your account, or your activity on it, doesn’t follow our rules.”

“We suspended your page. This is because Russell Brand goes against our community standards,” reads the screenshot from Brand’s now-removed Instagram profile page.

Related Stories

Jon Stewart Slams Haley Stevens’ Mike Rogers Endorsement Ahead of Election Day

Jon Stewart Trolls Trump’s Nicki Minaj Fixation After ‘Beautiful Ass’ Comment: ‘He’s Like Yogi Bear Floating Towards a Pie’

The British comedian was sentenced Monday to 10 years and six months in prison after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Brand’s X page, with 10 million followers, is still active. “There never was a Russell Brand, according to @Meta . Thank God for @elonmusk . Stay tuned,” he wrote on X Wednesday.

Brand’s account was taken down because it “violates our policies,” a Meta spokesperson confirmed to TMZ .

After Brand’s comedy and movie appearances tapered off, he started a YouTube channel which during the COVID pandemic became increasingly right-wing and full of conspiracy theories.

He was accused of sexual misconduct multiple times before finally being charged in 2025. In 2023, YouTube suspended monetization of his account.

Judge Joel Bennathan began his sentencing remarks Monday by saying, “About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous. You were clever and, in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator.”

“No doubt your companions thought it was outrageous laddish behavior that only you could get away with: It was outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal sexual offense, and as it turns out you haven’t got away with it,” the judge noted.

London’s Metropolitan Police said that Brand is being investigated on further allegations of rape from two other women.

article_text:
Source: Busan International Film Festival

Majid Majidi

Majid Majidi’s Iranian drama Midday Meal won the Busan Award for best film at the 31 st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) on Thursday (October 15) as the festival reported its biggest audience figures since 2015.

The film, about a teacher who becomes an oil smuggler to save his village school, wins a prize of $37,000 (KRW50m) and qualifies for submission to the Academy Awards in the best international feature film category. BIFF is the only Asia-based festival to offer such an incentive.

Scroll down for full list of winners

The trophy was presented by Zhang Lu, director of last year’s inaugural Competition winner Gloaming In Luomu , and jury president Zhang Yimou.

Taking to the stage at the Busan Cinema Center, Majidi expressed gratitude for receiving the honour in his first visit to South Korea. “The hero of our films is the audience,” he said. “It’s because of you that cinema is alive.” He dedicated the award to the “brave people of Iran” who are “still resisting against oppression” and “never give up”.

The film marks the first time Majidi has been invited to Busan, having previously played Cannes, Berlin and Venice over the past 35 years. He is Iran’s most submitted filmmaker to the international category of the Academy Awards, landing a nomination in 1999 with Children Of Heaven and making the shortlist in 2021 with Sun Children .

The ceremony also saw Taiwan’s Lee Yun Chan win best director for To Be Ordinary , a drama which follows the challenges a young man and his family face after he becomes paralysed in a car accident. The filmmaker was last at BIFF more than 20 years ago with debut The Shoe Fairy . Fellow Taiwanese filmmaker Shu Qi won the same award last year for Girl and was in attendance at tonight’s ceremony.

The special jury prize went to Ibuku , a mother-daughter drama by Indonesian filmmaker Eddie Cahyono. It proved a full circle moment for the director, who first presented the film at Busan’s Asian Project Market in 2015.

The Busan awards for best actor went to China’s Zhou Xun for her performance in Gu You’s The First Taste Of Loneliness and Japanese newcomer Kashun Himeno for her debut on-screen role in Shuichi Okita’s Satoko Always .

The First Taste Of Loneliness also picked up the Busan award for artistic contribution which went to sound designer Li Danfeng. His credits include 2025’s Resurrection , directed by BIFF Competition jury member Bi Gan.

Indian filmmaker Shashank Walia won the New Currents Award with his feature debut Birds In The Dark , the story of a police informant and the journey he takes with a man in his custody. It is the film’s second win at Busan after it was awarded the Songwon Vision Audience Award – Asia at a ceremony yesterday.

Acclaimed Chinese director Zhang Yimou presided over the Competition section jury, which also included Chinese director Bi Gan, South Korean actor Moon Choi, Japanese filmmaker Kei Ishikawa, Korean director July Jung, Vietnamese producer Tran Thi Bich Ngoc and Kazak actor Samal Yeslyamova.

The festival’s Vision Awards – for rising independent Asian filmmakers, playing in its Vision-Asia and Vision-Korea sections – were unveiled at a ceremony yesterday, led by Mongolian satire Zogsool by Sakhya Byamba .

Biggest attendance since 2015

A final report from BIFF revealed that total admissions to this year’s festival reached 200,043 – a 13.7% increase and more than 24,000 people than 2025 – to its total selection of 315 films (246 in official selection). This ranks as the festival’s biggest audience since 2015. A further 76,984 participants attended events held throughout Busan over the 10-day festival.

Organisers put the increase down to opening a day earlier than usual, with the festival beginning on a Tuesday rather than Wednesday, and an expanded screening programme.

The report also stated that the 21 st Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), which ran alongside the festival from October 10-13, drew a record 30,484 participants – up 1.5% on 2025.A total of 1,266 companies and 3,158 industry professionals from 58 countries attended, all slightly up on last year.

At the Busan Exhibitor and Convention Center (Bexco), ACFM hosted 339 companies from 32 countries across 129 booths. The market itself hosted 339 companies from 32 countries across 129 booths. This included 20 pavilions, with Czech, Slovak and Cambodia pavilions joining for the first time.

The Asian Project Market hosted 30 upcoming titles, with industry awards led by Tribeny Rai’s A Chronicle of Minor Things and Indonesian project Goldfish.

It marked the first year BIFF has taken place as an A-list festival, after gaining the status in March from the International Federation of Film Producers Associations (FIAPF), joining the likes of Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Sundance and Toronto.

Busan Awards 2026

Best film

Midday Meal , dir. Majid Majidi (Iran)

Best director

Lee Yun Chan, To Be Ordinary (Taiwan)

Special jury award

Ibuku , dir. Eddie Cahyono (Indo-Japan)

Best actor

Zhou Xun, The First Taste Of Loneliness (China)

Kashun Himeno, Satoko Always (Japan)

Artistic contribution award

Li Danfeng, sound director, The First Taste Of Loneliness (China)

BIFF Awards

New Currents award

Birds In The Dark , Shashank Walia (India)

BIFF Mecenat Award (Asia)

Agaar , dir. Yang Bo (China-Fr)

BIFF Mecenat Award (Korea)

Can I Talk To You? , dir. Yi Seungjun

Special mention : A Woman Dancing On The Waves , dir. Choi Se-dam

Sonje Award (Asia)

Fatima , dir. Soroush Shahpouri (Iran

Sonja Award (Korea)

Toe’s , dir. Yun Taerang

Special mention : The Boy Who Fell To Earth, dir. Jung Jaeseo

article_text:
Bill Pullman , Seth Rogen and Lauren Miller Rogen , Peter Farrelly , Luke Davies and Stephen Beresford will join Jessica Lange as honorees set for this year’s Sun Valley Film Festival , which runs December 2-6

The fest revealed its kudos list as well as its lineup Wednesday, with awards-buzzy films led by I Play Rocky , All of a Sudden , The Debut , Elsinore , Everybody Digs Bill Evans , Long Day’s Journey Into Night , A Long Winter , The Row , Tangles, Ink, Artificial and Tenzing among those heading to the resort town.

Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut will open the festival, while Luca Guadagnino’s OpenAI tale Artificial will close it. The fest also will screen 30 short films across its five-day run.

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Jessica Lange To Receive Vision Award At Sun Valley Film Festival

‘Tangles’ Cast Members Seth Rogen, Julia Louis-Dreyfus & Bryan Cranston On Animated Film’s Rare Back Story

“This year’s lineup brings together artists who have shaped film and television across generations, from Jessica Lange and Bill Pullman to Peter Farrelly,” said Teddy Grennan, the festival’s executive director and co-founder. “Sun Valley is a place where audiences can get close to the craft, whether through a screening, a Coffee Talk or a conversation over dinner, and we’re thrilled to welcome these remarkable talents to the mountains this December.”

Pullman, in town along with a screening of his jazz drama Everybody Digs Bill Evans , will receive the fest’s Pioneer Award, while Rogen and Miller Rogen will be bestowed the Impact Award alongside a screening of their latest work as producers, the animated Tangled ; both awards recognize contributions to film and the entertainment industry. Farrelly will participate in a Q&A on December 5 after the fest’s screening of I Play Rocky , his pic about the making of Sylvester Stallone’s 1976 boxing epic.

Deadline behind a pair of SVFF’s awards this year. Davies, who penned the script for Apple Original Films’ Mount Everest tale Tenzing , will receive the Deadline Disruptor Award, while screenwriter-playwright Beresford, who penned Focus Features’ Elsinore , will receive the High Scribe Award, co-presented by Deadline, for his contributions to screenwriting and ability to bring compelling, deeply human stories to the screen.

As Deadline previously reported, Lange will receive the SVFF’s Vision Award on December 4 at the Vision Award Dinner. Her film Long Day’s Journey Into Night , starring Lange and Ed Harris, will screen at the fest December 3.

article_text:
“Our business and our business flywheel are working. There is no need for a fundamental shift in the strategy. We do need better execution in the U.S. Our content around the world is largely working,” Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos insisted Tuesday as analysts lobbed question upon question about what the company is doing to address a slowdown in growth.

In other words, strong titles in global territories from Asia Pacific to Latin America are driving engagement, subscriber growth, revenue and profit. “The U.S. is also working, it’s just not growing as fast as it could, or as fast as we’d like. We had some really solid doubles and triples this year, but the other territories count on some of those titles being home runs so that they’ll travel around the world,” he said on a call after quarterly earnings . “We’re focusing on that execution.”

Related Stories

Netflix Stock Falls Despite Solid Q3 Results On Lowered Advertising Guidance, Disappointing Revenue Outlook

Skeptical Wall Street Dings Netflix On Soft Revenue Forecast

He’ll be leaning for that in large part on new chief content officer Peter Rice to lead that charge.

Watch on Deadline

“Our strategy is unchanged,” he said at another point, focused on originals combined with licensed fare and a growing live business. He somewhat dismissed short-form video and third-party or user-generated content that some Wall Streeters think could help boost engagement as “early-stage initiatives” with limited investment.

He did say to expect more deals like the one with TF1 network in France that brings strong local programming onto the platform.

The job of co-CEOs Sarandos and Greg Peters on the video call today was to reassure investors – who have bid the stock down over 40% in the last year – that there’s a path to long-term growth. On one hand, the streamer’s bid for Warner Bros., massive job cuts and C-suite changes indicate a recognition that change is needed in a fiercely competitive market. On the other, the CEOs reassured the Street that the solution is, while not easy, rather simple, that it mostly needs to deliver enough “quality and quantity” of programming consistently. That’s the slate, and they said it looks stronger this fall and into next year and that Netflix aims to keep it that way.

Sarandos said the streamer sees overall engagement “as the sum total of actual value that we are delivering to members… And the best evidence that we’ve got that we’re delivering that value is churn.” Netflix in fact leads all of its rivals in customer retention.

“Q3 churn, both globally and in the United States, improved year on year. It’s better than forecast. It’s already industry leading. And the ultimate determinant of whether we are delivering that value is the reaction to price changes” – meaning the streamer’s recent subscription price hikes have gone well.

Netflix CFO Spencer Neumann said the focus is firmly on the key metrics of member growth, pricing, and ads. “And we expect to deliver strong revenue growth into 2027 as well with those same three levers. The ad side led to softer-than-anticipated revenue guidance for full-year 2026 that dinged the shares today, when they fell 6% after the close.

Theatrical is another area but the strategy there is still a bit confusing. Netflix is planning to release 30 films theatrically this year from small platform releases with long windows, to wide family films. It just started reporting box office with La Bola Negra this past weekend.

“We are a streaming-first business. That is our core. But we consider every time we have a new film, the film itself, the audience for the film, and the filmmaker when we’re trying to come up with the release plan,” Sarandos said.

“We start off by looking at the project we have, asking ourselves how do we best serve movie lovers, many of whom are our members, who want to see that movie in a theater, and how do we do it without actually harming the view value on Netflix?”

La Bola Negra opened well in limited release. “We’re really excited about where we sit now, of course, we have one week of public reporting of box office under our belt, and we’re real happy about it. Let’s check in again in about six months,” Sarandos said.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "自29日起，肯·拉塞尔（Ken Russell）于1970年推出的狂热历史片将以修复版形式重返大银幕。这部作品以17世纪法国一座修女院以及一名被指控犯有巫术的牧师周围发生的震撼事件为基础，曾在当年引发丑闻，但如今非常值得重新发现。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "几乎没有哪位电影导演能像肯·拉塞尔那样以如此狂野的影像进行思考。如果去寻找同等物，最有可能在造型艺术的极端表现中找到：野兽派、巴洛克、波普艺术。拉塞尔脑海中诞生的东西是一种狂喜。当你观看这位生于1927年、卒于2011年的英国电影人为BBC电视或电影院创作的众多电影化艺术家传记时，必须了解这一点。关于马勒、柴可夫斯基、埃尔加或戴留斯。谁若在这里期待说教，必将感到失望，甚至受到震撼。拉塞尔从不手拿历史书进行思考，他迷失在潜意识之中；他从不机械核对事实，而是竭尽全力从自己的视角去表达作品和艺术家的本质。", "links": [{"text": "Ken Russell", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/person/details/216/ken-russell"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "画面常常与他一同奔驰，凝聚成一种狂热的状态，这种状态与真实事件的关系较小，而更多地与观察对象在被称为肯·拉塞尔的混乱“黑匣子”中触发的东西有关。难怪他因此常常遭到敌意相向，被指控进行精神强暴——例如，当他仅通过对妻子妮娜·米库洛娃（Nina Mikulowa）失败的爱以及对自我的执着之爱来定义柴可夫斯基，或是将马勒置于宗教和政治狂热的包围圈中进行过度夸张时。拉塞尔拥有一种天赋，能够仿佛直接将脑海中那些荒诞的（梦幻）画面烧灼到银幕上。这有时或许显得下流或越界，但它也提供了超越纯粹模仿真实事件的探讨与接近方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "对一桩骇人听闻的历史事件的重新审视", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这也适用于他的历史片《恶魔》（1970）。“本片基于历史事实。其主要人物确有其原型，而影片所描述的主要事件也确实发生过”：这段引言式的说明在开场时以巨大的猩红色全屏大字醒目地印在变形宽银幕（Scope）上，让接下来近两个小时内所能看到的影像显得更加骇人听闻。提供这一素材的是阿道司·赫胥黎（Aldous Huxley）的历史小说《卢丹的恶魔》（The Devils of Loudun）以及约翰·惠丁（John Whiting）于1960年为皇家莎士比亚剧团（Royal Shakespeare Company）创作的舞台改编剧本。", "links": [{"text": "Die Teufel", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/film/details/36965/die-teufel"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/bild/filmdb/379181/die-teufel-directors-cut-ken-russells-the-devils-plakat-cannes.jpg?t=1790947869", "alt": "2026年在戛纳首映：《恶魔》修复版", "caption": "2026年在戛纳首映：《恶魔》修复版（© Warner Bros. Discovery, Spencer Collantes)", "credit": "Filmdienst", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "曾经，这部电影只能以残缺的版本上映", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "肯·罗素那狂热的影像风格也让他备受攻击。在1970年代，对《魔鬼》的抵制极其剧烈。难怪早在电影上映前，甚至在影片获得“英国电影分级委员会”（BBFC）批准之前，就有删减建议被递交给导演。1971年2月，制作公司在一封给罗素的信中提出了十点意见，涉及对各种显露的（梦境）序列进行潜在删减。片中展现修道院内欲念宣泄以及伴随宗教裁判所发生的暴力行为的诸多细节，均应从电影中剪掉。首当其冲的是长达数分钟、宛如狂欢般的场景：受审讯者煽动、看似着魔的修女们将一尊巨大的十字架从祭坛上搬下，对救世主进行亵渎。随后的放映中，不仅缺了这段声名狼藉的“基督遭强暴”（Rape of Christ）序列，还有好几打其他镜头——其中部分长短不一——在首映前被制片厂联手BBFC从片中强行剔除。对罗素而言，对他的影像世界进行这样的干涉，本身就是对他艺术作品的亵渎。但最终他也是缚手束脚，影片只能删减版上映。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，即便这一删节版本也足以让《恶魔》在当时成为一部丑闻电影。正如早在15世纪就在教堂祭坛上绘制了同样狂热且挑衅的影像世界的耶罗尼米斯·博斯的作品一样，这部电影其实是不朽的艺术，这一点在当时常常被忽视。半个多世纪后，《恶魔》如今在修复版中迎来了新机遇，并将自29日起重返大片场。修复人员发现了被认为已经丢失的电影胶卷，并费力地将《恶魔》恢复到了肯·拉塞尔当年设想的状态。这是一部摄制于斯坦利·库布里克的《巴里·林登》问世四年前、且与《发条橙》同一年诞生的电影。这一切如今皆已成为公认的杰作。而肯·拉塞尔的《恶魔》完全有资格与它们相提并论", "links": [{"text": "Barry Lyndon", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/film/details/25931/barry-lyndon"}, {"text": "Uhrwerk Orange", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/film/details/51523/uhrwerk-orange"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
Ab 29. Oktober kommt Ken Russells fiebriger Historienfilm aus dem Jahr 1970 in restaurierter Form zurück in die Kinos. Das auf schockierenden Begebenheiten rund um ein Nonnenkloster und einen der Hexerei angeklagten Priester im Frankreich des 17. Jahrhunderts fußende Werk sorgte seinerzeit für einen Skandal, lohnt aber die Wiederentdeckung.

Kaum ein Filmregisseur denkt in so wilden Bildern wie Ken Russell . Sucht man nach Äquivalenzen, wird man am ehesten in den Extremen der bildenden Kunst fündig: Fauvismus, Barock, Pop Art. Was Russells Kopf gebiert, ist ein Rausch. Das muss man wissen, wenn man etwa die mannigfaltigen filmischen Künstlerbiografien anschaut, die der 1927 geborene, 2011 verstorbene britische Filmemacher fürs Fernsehen der BBC oder fürs Kino produziert hat. Über Mahler, Tschaikowski, Elgar oder Delius. Wer hier Didaktisches erwartet, wird enttäuscht, ja erschüttert werden. Russell denkt nicht mit dem Geschichtsbuch in der Hand, er verliert sich im Unterbewusstsein; er klappert keine Fakten ab, sondern ringt darum, dem Wesen von Werk und Künstler aus eigener Perspektive Ausdruck zu verleihen.

Häufig gehen die Bilder mit ihm durch, verdichten sich zu rauschhaften Zuständen, die weniger etwas mit wahren Begebenheiten zu tun haben als mit dem, was der Betrachtungsgegenstand in der wirren „Blackbox“ namens Ken Russell triggert. Kein Wunder, dass er dafür oft angefeindet wird, dass man ihn der geistigen Vergewaltigung bezichtigt, wenn er etwa Tschaikowski nur über die scheiternde Liebe zu seiner Frau Nina Mikulowa und die obsessive Liebe zu sich selbst definiert oder Mahler im Bannkreis von religiösem und politischem Fanatismus überzeichnet. Russell hat die Gabe, die absurden (Traum-)Bilder aus seinem Kopf scheinbar direkt auf die Leinwand zu brennen. Das mag mitunter obszön sein oder übergriffig, doch es bietet auch Auseinandersetzung und Annäherungen über das pure Nachstellen von verbürgten Gegebenheiten hinaus.

Die Aufarbeitung einer ungeheuerlichen historischen Begebenheit

Das gilt auch für seinen Historienfilm „ Die Teufel “ (1970). „Dieser Film basiert auf historischen Fakten. Dessen Hauptcharaktere haben wirklich gelebt, und die wesentlichen Ereignisse, die der Film beschreibt, sind tatsächlich passiert“: Diese einführende Erläuterung prankt zu Beginn in Karminrot in riesigen Lettern bildfüllend auf der Scope-Leinwand – und lässt das, was in den nächsten knapp zwei Stunden zu sehen sein wird, umso ungeheuerlicher wirken. Die Basis dafür lieferten Russell Aldous Huxleys historischer Roman „Die Teufel von Loudun“ und dessen Bühnen-Adaption, die John Whiting 1960 für die Royal Shakespeare Company verfasst hatte.

Der Stoff fußt auf realen Begebenheiten des Jahres 1633, als einige Nonnen des Klosters der Ursulinen von Loudun ihren Priester Urbain Grandier beschuldigten, sie verhext zu haben. Er, seinerzeit ein politischer Freigeist und Verfechter der Rechte einer von König Ludwig XIII. und Kirche unabhängigen Stadt Loudun, wurde von Kardinal Richelieu der Ketzerei und Hexerei angeklagt und in einem von „Teufelsaustreibungen“ und „hochnotpeinlichen Befragungen“ begleiteten Prozess zum Tode auf dem Scheiterhaufen verurteilt. Soweit die Fakten.

Pervertiertes Begehren und politische Machtdemonstration

„Die Religionskriege sind vorbei! Katholiken wenden sich nicht mehr gegen Protestanten. Wir haben überlebt. Und wir verdanken unser Überleben der Weisheit und der Menschlichkeit.“ Mit diesen Worten führt Ken Russell seinen frommen Freigeist Urbain Grandier ein, der vor den weiß gekachelten Mauern seiner Klosterfestung die Bevölkerung von Loudun auf die Freiheit einschwört. Das Setting, für das der spätere Meisterregisseur Derek Jarman als Szenenbildner verantwortlich zeichnet, erinnert an eine aseptische, einem riesigen Schwimmbad entwachsen scheinende Trutzburg, von der man nicht glauben möchte, dass sich hinter ihren unschuldig weißen Mauern die moralischen Abgründe auftun werden, die dann später der Staats- und Kirchenmacht den Vorwand dazu liefern werden, ihren grausigen Prozess zu vollführen. Zu den Klängen des gregorianischen „Dies Irae“ wandert die Prozession in die Stadt. An der Spitze der stattliche Grandier. Ken Russell hat ihn mit dem seinerzeit markigen Frauenschwarm Oliver Reed besetzt. Kein Wunder, galt Grandier doch als ein Mann, der den Frauen nicht abgeneigt war. Und so geben sich die Nonnen auch alle Mühe, den ein oder anderen Blick durch die vergitterten Luken des Klosters zu erhaschen. Der Ton ist gesetzt.

Noch dominiert zwar das Schwarz-weiß der Gewänder und der Gemäuer. Doch bald wird klar: Ken Russell ist hier angetreten, um zu blenden, zu schwelgen, zu geißeln – und vor allem keine Gefangenen zu machen. Seine den Ursulinen vorstehende Äbtissin Jeanne ist verschlagen und verbirgt ihre Boshaftigkeit und ihr Begehren nach Grandier hinter der Contenance einer strenggläubigen Dienerin Gottes. Russell zeigt sie als Figur mit schlanker Gestalt und schönem Gesicht, aber auch einem Buckel und einem schiefen Hals: dezent zu sein war nie eine Eigenschaft des Regisseurs und Drehbuchautors. Jeanne ist bei ihm die wahre Teufelin der Geschichte, die Grandier ins Unglück stürzen wird. Und Vanessa Redgrave spielt sie mit einer Inbrunst, die schaudern lässt.

Talent vor und hinter der Kamera

Sowieso hat Russell fürs Ensemble seines Satanswerk nur die Besten ausgesucht. Neben Reed und Redgrave ist Dudley Sutton als Baron de Laubardemont zu sehen, Advokat der Inquisition, sowie Georgina Hale als Grandiers Mätresse. Hinter der Kamera wirkten neben Derek Jarman als Setdesigner unter anderem „Oscar“-Preisträger David Watkin („Jenseits von Afrika“) an der Kamera und vor allem Avantgarde-Komponist Peter Maxwell Davies mit, der bis Mitte der 1980er-Jahre die britische Orchestermusik prägte und mit dem Soundtrack zu „Die Teufel“ sein einzig maßgebliches filmmusikalisches Werk schuf.

Das „Die Irae“ verzerrt Maxwell Davies im Prolog zu „Die Teufel“ zu einem schrägen Bläsergewitter und markiert mit seiner Atonalität – der Film hat da noch nicht Zeit gehabt, Luft zu holen – eine erste fiebrige Traumsequenz, in der Grandier in goldbesticktem Leinen wie Jesus übers Wasser wandelt, bis zur nur mit einem Unterhemd und ihren langen roten Haaren bedeckt am Ufer wartenden Jeanne, die dem Ankömmling ergeben die Füße küsst. Diese surreale Szene, in der sich Jeannes unterdrücktes sexuelles Begehren die Gestalt religiöser Inbrunst gibt, gehört noch zu den dezenteren Kopfgeburten Russells, der im Folgenden noch weit expliziter und ungehöriger gegen kirchliche Bigotterie, vor allem aber auch gegen das autoritäre Bündnis der Kirche mit dem Staat sticheln wird.

„Schaut mich nicht an. Schaut auf eure Stadt“, brüllt Grandier am Ende auf dem Scheiterhaufen, während er verkohlt. „Wenn eure Stadt erst zerstört sein wird, hat eure Freiheit auch ein Ende! Würdet ihr doch nur freie Menschen bleiben. Ihr könntet kämpfen. Oder ihr werdet Sklaven werden.“ Sie hören nicht, und mit dem letzten Wimmern des Geistlichen zerbersten die weißen Mauern der Stadt.

Einst kam der Film nur verstümmelt ins Kino

Seine Bilderwut hat Ken Russell auch angreifbar gemacht. Der Widerstand gegen „Die Teufel“ war in den 1970er-Jahren immens. Kein Wunder, dass bereits vor der Veröffentlichung, ja bereits vor der Freigabe des Films durch das „British Board of Film Classification“ (BBFC) Kürzungsvorschläge an den Regisseur herangetragen wurden. Im Februar 1971 wurden zehn Punkte von Seiten des Produktionsstudios in einem Brief an Russell offenbar, mögliche Kürzungen diverser expliziter (Traum-)Sequenzen betreffend. Etliche Details, in denen die Auslebung der Lust innerhalb des Klosters und Gewalttaten im Zuge der Inquisition visualisiert wurden, sollten aus dem Film geschnitten werden. Allen voran eine lange, orgiengleiche Szene, in der durch die Befrager aufgeputschte, besessen scheinende Nonnen ein riesiges Kruzifix vom Altar holen, um sich an dem Heiland zu vergehen. Diese berüchtigte „Rape of Christ“-Sequenz fehlte im Folgenden wie auch gut zwei Dutzend weitere, zum Teil viel kürzere Einstellungen, die das Studio zusammen mit der BBFC aus dem Film noch vor seiner Premiere entfernen ließ. Für Russell war ein derartiger Eingriff in seine Bilderwelten seinerseits ein Sakrileg an seinem Kunstwerk. Letztendlich waren ihm aber die Hände gebunden, und der Film kam nur gekürzt zur Aufführung.

Doch auch diese gekürzte Fassung reichte aus, um „Die Teufel“ seinerzeit zum Skandalfilm zu machen. Dass der Film, wie einst die Werke von Hieronymus Bosch, der bereits im 15. Jahrhundert ähnlich fiebrig-provokante Bilderwelten an die Altäre der Kirchen malte, tatsächlich bleibende Kunst ist, wurde damals oft übersehen. Mehr als ein halbes Jahrhundert später bekommt „Die Teufel“ nun in restaurierter Fassung eine neue Chance und kommt ab 29. Oktober zurück in die Kinos. Restauratoren haben verloren geglaubte Filmrollen entdeckt und „Die Teufel“ mühevoll in jenen Stand zurückversetzt, der Ken Russell einst vorschwebte. Ein Film, der vier Jahre vor Stanley Kubricks „ Barry Lyndon “ und im gleichen Jahr wie „ Uhrwerk Orange “ entstand. Alles inzwischen anerkannte Meisterwerke. Und „Die Teufel“ von Ken Russell hat es verdient, im gleichen Atemzug genannt zu werden

article_text:
Sponsored

Fieldwork as Form: The International Ethnographic Triennial

Bison and associated Upper Paleolithic artifacts, ca. 20,000–22,000 BCE.

Around 22,000 years ago, a small bison figurine was carved from mammoth ivory in what is now Zaraysk, a town roughly 100 kilometers southeast of Moscow. At just 10 centimeters, the object is among the oldest figurative sculptures known to exist. It is also the starting point for the International Ethnographic Triennial (IET), organized by the National Centre “Russia,” a project that launched in Zaraysk this past summer and is building toward a main exhibition in 2030.

Conceived as an encounter between contemporary art practice and the discipline of anthropology, the Triennial is currently in the midst of a multi-year research phase. For the next several years, artists, curators, anthropologists, filmmakers, and museum specialists from various countries will conduct field expeditions, collaborate with regional ethnographic and local-history institutions, and develop international expert and curatorial councils. The project will also unfold an extensive programme including exhibitions, research, educational courses and expeditions. Its aim is to create a space in which artistic and scientific practices will allow a fresh look at cultural heritage and reveal points of contact between different societies and traditions.

Left: ELENA YUSHINA , Head of the Exhibition and Curatorial Department, National Centre “Russia,” (TBC), and NATALIA VIRTUOZOVA , Director General, National Centre “Russia,” and Commissioner of the International Ethnographic Triennial, with participants. Right: MEHRET MANDEFRO , co-curator of the International Ethnographic Triennial, with participants, at the meeting of the International Ethnographic Triennial, Zaraysk, 2026.

Zaraysk holds a rare compression of historical layers: at its base, the Upper Paleolithic, represented by the bison and a group of small “Venus” figurines that represent some of humanity’s earliest attempts at image-making. Above that lie centuries of Russian regional life, and then the literary and sculptural associations of Dostoevsky, whose family estate lay in the surrounding district, and the sculptor Anna Golubkina, who was born in the town. IET Commissioner Natalia Virtuozova described the site as a place where “the memory of the human being has been preserved” across millennia, and framed the project’s purpose as comprehending that past while orienting toward the future.

Bison and associated Upper Paleolithic artifacts, ca. 20,000–22,000 BCE.

Mehret Mandefro (USA/Ethiopia), an anthropologist and filmmaker serving as one of the Triennial’s international co-curators, emphasized fieldwork as a discipline of presence rather than detachment: “Ethnographers do not simply observe another culture from the outside—they are in the midst of events, try the food, attend rituals, try to understand a way of life from within.” For the IET, the ethnographic approach is not a scholarly framework imposed on art but a shared mode of attention that art and research can inhabit together. Elena Yushina, who heads the IET’s curatorial department, elaborated that the project is “a living laboratory where anthropologists, artists, and museum specialists work side by side.”

When the main show opens in 2030, it will draw together contemporary artworks, field research outcomes, and archival and museum holdings, with a parallel public programme of discussions, screenings, and international conferences. The IET’s longer-term vision is to function as a sustained platform beyond 2030, maintaining networks among institutions, researchers, artists, and communities engaged with cultural memory, identity, and shared futures.

title_original: Crítica | Verity (2026): um suspense que não sai do rascunho
editorial_title_zh: 影评 | 《Verity》（2026年）：一部停留在草稿阶段的悬疑片
editorial_excerpt_zh: 安妮·海瑟薇表现亮眼，但这部改编自科琳·胡佛小说的电影堆砌了重重反转，却未能赋予角色以实质，也未能为他们的秘密营造紧张感。这篇文章《影评 | 《Verity》（2026年）：一部停留在草稿阶段的悬疑片》最早发布于 Cinema com Rapadura 。

"一个反转可能会彻底改变一个故事，但对于跟随故事的观众来说，它并不能改变太多东西。迈克尔·肖沃特在《 Verity 》中堆砌了种种惊喜，却忘记了观众需要先了解角色，才能感受到每一项发现所威胁要摧毁的东西有多大分量。相反，导演选择将悬疑感围绕在下一个隐藏的信息周围展开，从而抛开了本应让等待变得令人煎熬的不信任感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "洛温·阿什利（达科塔·约翰逊饰）在母亲去世后面临经济困难，此时她接到了一份工作：完成因车祸而无法继续写作的维里蒂·克劳福德（安妮·海瑟薇饰）的图书。她搬进这位女作家的家中，翻阅着笔记和草稿，直到找到了一份包含令人不安的自白的自传体手稿。在试图理解自己所阅读的内容的同时，洛温渐渐与维里蒂的丈夫杰瑞米（乔什·哈奈特饰）越走越近，并开始渴望过上一种她越来越有理由对其产生怀疑的生活。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尼克·安托斯卡根据科琳·胡佛的小说改编的剧本试图为这种吸引力建立理由，但对主角的刻画却缺乏实质内容。悲伤、职业上的不安全感以及获得物质慰藉的可能性，让这个提议充满了诱惑。然而，我们却无从得知洛温愿意为了占据那个空间而牺牲什么样的价值观。同时，从最初的那种脆弱感到洛温卷入这个家庭后所做出的种种选择之间，明显缺乏一条令人信服的演进脉络。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "促使她来到这里的写作本身，也得到了流于表面的处理。影片几乎没有表现出成为小说家对洛温意味着什么，也没有展现这段经历会如何干预她对这份手稿的解读。她基本上只是一个和观众一同接受这些发现的旁观者。达科塔·约翰逊的表演情感表达范围极窄，进一步加剧了这一局限性。面对好奇、欲望或恐惧时，她低沉的嗓音和隐忍的姿态几乎没有变化，极大地拉平了那些本该标志着洛温与其他人关系发生变化的反应之间的区别。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大段的阅读桥段让这种局限性变得更加明显。当维里蒂接管手稿的旁白时，镜头不断执着地切回正在阅读的洛温、她的眼睛或她手中的纸张。情况本已明了，但电影却不断重复确认到底是谁在阅读，却未能从这些回切中找到能够改变叙事含义的反应，也未能探讨这些字眼对主角产生的影响。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "画面构图过于简单，导演对空间以及那些隐匿于视线之外的事物的探索也相当有限，同时还诉诸于可预测的惊吓桥段（jump scares）。就连该类型的典型俗套（例如明显与某个秘密相关联的湖泊）也未能对营造忧虑的氛围有所贡献。观众能察觉到有什么东西被隐藏了，却感受不到围绕着这一发现的不安。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当这些情节反转勉强激起一丝惊奇感时，随之而来的却是越来越缺乏说服力的解释。带有这些特征的素材如果采用更为公开的情节剧拍法，或者去支撑一部严肃的悬疑片，或许本能奏效。然而，《Verity》既没有找到一种能赋予这些夸张情节以力量的基调，也没有构建起让它们变得充满威胁感所需的紧张氛围。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "安妮·海瑟薇贡献了全片最厚重的表演，即便在剧本施加了种种限制、做出了难以立足的转变时，她依然赋予了角色强大的存在感。她的投入制造出了不少有趣的时刻，而导演却无法将这些时刻延续下去或融入整体之中。至于乔什·哈奈特，他拿到的是一个可预测的富有魅力的丈夫形象，其发展轨迹几乎不出意料。这位演员曾在《陷阱》中饰演过类似的角色，在那里，利用魅力影响他人的桥段同样反复出现，但却有着更为丰富的性格细微差别。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当电影试图重新审视书面自白的含义时，这种脆弱性就变得更加明显了。新的解释和它试图澄清的事件一样难以接受，而疑虑也开始依赖于任何信息都有可能被否定的这种可能性。这种模棱两可本可以丰富洛温的欲望与她选择相信的内容之间的关系。然而在这里，她的角色塑造却不足以支撑这种解读，从而让这个反转背负了它无法承受的责任。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "到头来，《Verity》要求观众付出更多去接受它的解释，却未能提供足够理由让观众去投入关怀其角色。对下一次发现的期待，渐渐变成了伴随着追看一个把每一次事实的新版本都视作足以重燃兴趣的故事而产生的一种疲惫。一切都可能在任何时刻发生改变，但几乎没有什么是真正重要的。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Anne Hathaway se destaca, mas a adaptação do livro de Colleen Hoover acumula revelações sem dar consistência aos personagens ou tensão aos seus segredos.

Uma revelação pode mudar tudo numa história sem mudar muita coisa para quem a acompanha. Michael Showalter acumula surpresas em “ Verity ”, mas esquece que é preciso conhecer os personagens para sentir o peso do que cada descoberta ameaça destruir. Em vez disso, o diretor prefere organizar o suspense em torno da próxima informação escondida, deixando de lado a desconfiança que deveria tornar a espera angustiante.

Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson) enfrenta dificuldades financeiras depois da morte da mãe quando recebe a proposta de finalizar os livros de Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway), incapacitada após um acidente de carro. Instalada na casa da escritora, ela examina anotações e rascunhos até encontrar um manuscrito autobiográfico com confissões perturbadoras. Ainda tentando compreender o que leu, Lowen acaba se aproximando de Jeremy (Josh Hartnett), marido de Verity, passando a desejar uma vida da qual tem cada vez mais motivos para desconfiar.

O roteiro de Nick Antosca, adaptado do livro de Colleen Hoover, tenta estabelecer razões para essa atração, mas fornece pouca consistência à protagonista. O luto, a insegurança profissional e a possibilidade de conforto material tornam a proposta tentadora. Porém, falta conhecer os valores que Lowen estaria disposta a comprometer para ocupar aquele espaço. É perceptível ainda a ausência de uma progressão convincente entre essa vulnerabilidade do início e as escolhas que Lowen faz após se envolver com a família.

A própria escrita, responsável por levá-la até ali, recebe um tratamento superficial. Há pouco interesse pelo que significa ser romancista para Lowen ou por como essa experiência poderia interferir na interpretação do manuscrito. Ela funciona principalmente como alguém que recebe as descobertas junto do público. Dakota Johnson acentua essa limitação com uma atuação de pouquíssimo alcance expressivo. A voz baixa e a postura contida variam pouco diante da curiosidade, do desejo ou do medo, reduzindo drasticamente as diferenças entre reações que deveriam marcar mudanças na relação de Lowen com os demais personagens.

As longas passagens de leitura tornam essa limitação ainda mais evidente. Enquanto Verity assume a narração do manuscrito, a direção retorna insistentemente a Lowen lendo, aos seus olhos ou ao papel em suas mãos. A situação já está compreendida, mas o filme continua reafirmando quem lê, sem encontrar nesses retornos uma reação que transforme o sentido do relato ou explore o efeito daquelas palavras sobre a protagonista.

Os enquadramentos são simplistas demais, e a direção pouco explora o espaço e aquilo que permanece fora de vista, além de recorrer a jump scares previsíveis. Nem os clichês típicos do gênero, como o lago claramente associado a um segredo, contribuem para criar um clima de apreensão. O público percebe que há algo escondido, mas não sente a inquietude em torno da descoberta.

Quando as reviravoltas conseguem registrar uma nota de surpresa, vêm acompanhadas de explicações cada vez menos convincentes. Um material com essas características poderia funcionar sob uma condução mais abertamente melodramática ou sustentar um suspense sério. “Verity”, porém, não encontra um tom que dê força aos excessos nem constrói a tensão necessária para torná-los ameaçadores.

Anne Hathaway oferece a atuação mais densa do elenco, dando presença à personagem mesmo quando o roteiro impõe limites e mudanças difíceis de sustentar. Seu comprometimento produz momentos de interesse que a direção não consegue prolongar ou integrar ao conjunto. Josh Hartnett, por sua vez, recebe a figura previsível do marido sedutor, com um percurso que pouco se afasta do esperado. O próprio ator desempenhou um papel semelhante em “Armadilha” , em que o uso do charme para influenciar os outros se repete, mas com muito mais nuances de personalidade.

A fragilidade se torna mais evidente quando o filme tenta reconsiderar o sentido da confissão escrita. A nova explicação é tão difícil de aceitar quanto os acontecimentos que pretende esclarecer, e a dúvida passa a depender da possibilidade de qualquer informação ser desmentida. Essa ambiguidade poderia enriquecer a relação entre o desejo de Lowen e aquilo em que ela escolhe acreditar. Aqui, porém, sua caracterização é insuficiente para sustentar essa leitura, deixando a reviravolta com mais responsabilidade do que consegue assumir.

Ao fim, “Verity” exige mais disposição para aceitar suas explicações do que oferece motivos para se envolver com seus personagens. A expectativa pela próxima descoberta vai cedendo ao cansaço de acompanhar uma história que trata cada nova versão dos fatos como suficiente para renovar o interesse. Tudo pode mudar a qualquer momento, mas quase nada chega a importar.

article_text:
Source: Architect, HanWay, Blue Finch, Protagonist Pictures

Calum Gray, Gabrielle Stewart, Mike Chapman, Sarah Lebutsch

This year’s American Film Market (AFM), which runs from November 10-15, is taking place at an interesting juncture for independent film.

Distinctive films such as Black Bear’s medieval fisherwoman comedy Wicker , Laika’s Wildwood and A24’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything are outperforming expectations at the box office across the globe , and providing grounds for optimism.

“I definitely see the return of sophistication. The return of the frictive, of the singular, of the controversial,” says Architect Film Sales co-founder Calum Gray, whose slate includes Australian horror Wolf Cre3k.

But at the same time, as Netflix lays off 6% of its staff amid a tumbling stock price, and two huge buyers in Warner Bros and Paramount consolidate into the single Skydance entity, there are concerns that challenges lie ahead.

“I’m interested to see what Skydance does to the pay-TV landscape in the US. Losing one of those buyers isn’t going to be great – that’s not going to happen immediately, but I wonder if they’ll merge the teams… I’m interested to stress test how the US buyers are feeling,” adds Gray.

Despite the changes at Netflix, some sellers can see positive movement in the market from streamers.

Gray suggests the move into an advertising-based video on demand (AVoD) model means players including Netflix and Amazon need to re-focus on quality content, as opposed to quantity, which could be a good thing for the independents.

“By using AVoD metrics on retention rather than first click, [streamers] become a lot choosier because their business models change. A metric of retention just puts the bar up for us. We have to deliver things which hold an audience, which are distinctive conceptually, are packaged right.”

“What we need is for the streamers to support theatrical distributors’ releases by actively buying that pay-one [window] rather than self-generating,” adds Gabrielle Stewart, CEO of HanWay Films, which is launching Argentinian filmmaking duo Mariano Cohn and Gastón Duprat’s Mare Nostrum and Italian romantic comedy Honeymooners at AFM. “I see signs that they do.”

“It’s the least sexy market”

There is a solid showing from UK sales agents at this year’s AFM. While taking full-fat teams with all the marketing and acquisitions departments is no longer financially viable for most, the sales teams will be out in full force.

Some UK sellers have opted for a shared office space once again, this year housing Altitude, Blue Finch, Reason8, Screenbound, Celsius and The Mise en Scene Company.

UK sellers were delighted at how last year’s Fairmont Century Plaza venue worked out, closely located to the CAA, UTA and WME offices, after a few years of discombobulating venue-hopping. And with more restaurants understood to be opening this year at the back of the Fairmont building, the sellers are eager to get back.

Source: Fairmont Century Plaza

Fairmont Century Plaza

“It was my favourite market of last year because it is so well organised,” says Gray. “Efficient screening facilities, restaurants close to the main drag.”

“I can feel there’s so much more engagement from the agencies, the financiers [at the Fairmont]. AFM’s role in terms of connecting us to LA in business is there. When we were at Santa Monica, we were disconnected from the heart of the business,” says Stewart.

“It’s the least sexy one, compared to Berlin and Cannes and Toronto,” admits Mike Chapman, managing director of Blue Finch Films, which is selling horror thriller American Dollhouse at the market. “I’m hoping it will be like last year, which was very stable business, no major mess-ups, just all went to plan. It’s efficient, and all we need the market to be is efficient.”

“For the right packages, it is a good pre-sales market,” adds Protagonist Pictures’ new head of sales Sarah Lebutsch of AFM. The company will talk to buyers about its new packages: comedy It’s Alright starring and co-written by Paul Bettany and Robin Hood story The Lie Of Sherwood Forest.

“The big buyers are coming, and they are pre-buying there because, for better or worse, there isn’t the distraction of a festival.”

She does caveat that despite the range of US indie buyers that are growing in presence, from 1-2 Special to Angel Studios, that space remains tough for pre-sales. “It is probably a part of the world where pre-sales have become less prevalent, and we tend to sell more either off footage or on completion. But it’s not impossible.”

Engaging with buyers

On the international buyer side, a few absences have been noted. Some Australians are understood to have sat this year out. Middle Eastern buyers will be engaging remotely, although the region is perceived to be difficult to sell into right now, with the ongoing conflicts impacting buying power.

“A lot of those TV [deals] are linked to government budgets, so they have been forced to tighten those belts,” says Gray. “Some of those buyers are suffering a bit. I’m very sorry for that.”

Toronto’s inaugural market in September has also had an impact.

“There were a few buyers who went to Toronto expecting it to be more of a market and as a result aren’t coming to the AFM,” says Chapman. “Toronto is very expensive, AFM is very expensive, there are certain buyers from Latin America or Europe who are only doing one or the other.”

HanWay is prepared to engage remotely with such buyers.

“We are going to have a filmmaker event showing promos and filmmaker presentations,” explains Stewart. “We make sure that everyone attending is rewarded and gets to see it first, but then we make it available on a link because not everyone chooses to attend, and I understand that everyone’s having to make some financial decisions.”

For those buyers who did attend Toronto and will now be at AFM, any disappointments at the former could bring upsides for the latter. “Every buyer I’ve spoken to out of Toronto did not pick up very much that was playing in the festival. Maybe that means there’ll be more hunger at AFM,” suggests Chapman.

For Chapman, whose company is focused on genre titles, AFM comes at a useful point in the year. “We have a lot of films that either premiere or play at the key genre festivals around AFM. Beyond Fest has become more and more important to us. Having something premiere at Beyond and then being able to follow up with buyers at AFM is perfect timing. Sitges is around the same time, as is Fantastic Fest.”

Political shift

US politics will undoubtedly be a key talking point at AFM for local and international industry. It is the first major market since US lawmakers introduced a federal bill for a 20% transferable tax credit that will apply to above-the-line actors and directors as well as below-the-line workers.

“I’m delighted,” says Gray. “It will mean greater viability of finance plans coming out of the US, certainly for the lower and mid-level. We like good producers being able to greenlight more.”

“It’s a game changer for any films that you’re setting up in the US,” adds Stewart. “It’s an extra 20%, but at the same time, how much of it will be absorbed by talent agents asking for higher fees for their clients, because it encompasses above the line?

“I just hope that everyone approaches it holistically and continues to appreciate that they’ve got to support independent film,” she continues. “The biggest challenge is availability of talent and holding on to talent, because if they get offered a big paycheque from Netflix or Amazon, they’ll jump. And if that federal tax incentive is available for an Amazon series, and they’re going to manage to make it cheaper, they’ll probably pay the talent the extra, in a way that an independent film can’t. That balance of power isn’t going to change. It might even be increased.”

There is also the Democrats’ huge success in the US mid-term elections, which it is hoped will help bring about more global political and economic stability after an erratic two years under Donald Trump’s second presidential term. Whether the positive knock-on effect will be felt so quickly at AFM, no one can be sure.

“Most of the independent film industry will probably be feeling positively encouraged by these results, so it can only lighten the mood,” says Lebutsch.

“Republicans are blaming the war in Iran for the cost-of-living crisis, and it’s impacted the world’s cost-of-living crisis,” adds Stewart. “The fact that we can all feel incredibly certain that ending the war in Iran is of paramount importance now in America, that will take a lot of global pressure off everyone – cost of living, businesses. It has given us all a little boost.”

article_text:
Andy Serkis opened up recently about returning to the character that made him famous. Serkis not only plays Gollum again in the upcoming The Hunt for Gollum , he’s directing the film.

In a new interview with the Times , he held forth on the challenge of reviving his fan-favorite Lord of the Rings character, and the toll it took.

Related Stories

Andy Serkis Directs ‘The Hunt For Gollum’ In Character: See The Set Footage

‘Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power’ Action-Packed Season 3 Trailer Reveals Sauron’s Dark Dominance Over Middle-Earth

“I’ve just lived with Gollum for such a long period. I’m a terrible sleeper. My mind is pretty active, and it has been insane going back to the character I started playing 26 years ago, and so I’m waking up at night,” the actor revealed. “Actually, I don’t know if I’m asleep or awake, but I think, Am I directing you, Gollum? Or you me? Are we arguing?’ My mind is…busy.”

Earlier this week in an interview promoting his new book My Pressures , Serkis spoke about how a character changes the actor who inhabits them.

Watch on Deadline

“I’ve always believed and I still do believe that you’re always altered by the characters that you played as an actor, that you learn something either about yourself or the world that changes your worldview.

“I think you are kind of chemically changed in some way. You are tricking your body and your mind and your head and your psyche to fit this other being.”

He then added a thought that jives with his take on returning to the LOTR creature: “Sometimes decompressing from a character can take a long time.”

In the case of Gollum, that process may never be complete.

“I don’t suspect that Gollum will ever leave me, quite frankly,” he said.

article_text:
Durante i giorni di Artissima 2026 a Torino , l’incontro con le diverse declinazioni della creatività contemporanea si estende ben oltre la sede della fiera all’Oval. Dal 30 ottobre al 1° novembre TAG – Torino Art Galleries , associazione nata nel 2000 e oggi composta da 16 gallerie, propone aperture straordinarie, colazioni, nuove sedi e mostre diffuse in diversi quartieri della città. Il momento centrale sarà la TAG Art Night – Notte delle Arti Contemporanee, in programma sabato, 31 ottobre 2026, dalle 18 alle 23, con l’apertura serale straordinaria delle gallerie aderenti. A questa si affiancano le TAG Art Coffee Breakfast, previste venerdì 30, sabato 31 ottobre e domenica 1° novembre dalle 10 alle 12, occasioni per visitare le mostre davanti a una colazione, magari prima di raggiungere la fiera o di proseguire il lungo giro d’arte. L’ingresso agli appuntamenti è libero.

L’edizione coincide anche con alcuni passaggi significativi per la scena cittadina. Photo & Contemporary celebra trent’anni di attività con Lights & Shadows. Part Two , mentre Mazzoleni festeggia i quarant’anni con una mostra dedicata a Giorgio de Chirico . Galleria Umberto Benappi apre in anteprima oltre 700 metri quadrati negli spazi dell’ex Tuxedo di via Belfiore 8 con Join me in the underground , mentre Simóndi trasferisce la propria attività a Palazzo Scaglia di Verrua. Anche Riccardo Costantini inaugura un nuovo capitolo con Seconda Soluzione , che debutta in via Luigi Mercantini 5 con Turning Time Around .

«La TAG Art Night e le TAG Art Coffee Breakfast sono occasioni in cui le gallerie escono dalla dimensione del singolo spazio e diventano parte di un’esperienza condivisa della città», spiega il presidente di TAG Umberto Benappi , sottolineando l’obiettivo di rafforzare le relazioni tra galleristi, artisti, collezionisti, pubblico e territorio.

Dal centro storico a Borgo Nuovo

Il primo itinerario attraversa il centro di Torino partendo da Mazzoleni , in piazza Solferino, dove Giorgio de Chirico. Enigma contemporaneo mette in relazione il pictor optimus con Alberto Savinio, Luciano Fabro, Giulio Paolini, Salvo, Nunzio, Massimo Vitali, Marinella Senatore, Andrea Francolino e Iran do Espírito Santo.

Pochi minuti separano Mazzoleni da Tucci Russo Chambres d’Art , che presenta Harald Klingelhöller – and the world apart, twice (horizont) – , progetto dedicato al rapporto tra scultura e linguaggio. Poco distante, Seconda Soluzione inaugura la propria sede con Turning Time Around , collettiva che segna il passaggio verso la nuova identità della galleria. L’itinerario prosegue da Weber & Weber , dove How Slowly Can I Write? di Federica Patera e Andrea Sbra Perego, a cura di Barbara Pavan, trasforma la scrittura in materia tessile e scultorea.

A Palazzo Scaglia di Verrua convivono invece due gallerie TAG. Giorgio Persano presenta Siamo esseri singolari di Renato Maestri, con sculture e disegni degli anni Ottanta, mentre Simóndi inaugura nella nuova sede Inspira. Trattieni. Espira. Capitolo 2 , progetto costruito intorno ai temi della contemplazione, del rallentamento e della presenza.

Da qui si raggiunge Galleria Accademia Torino , con Enrico Baj: trame e passamanerie del disordine , dedicata alle superfici ironiche e materiche dell’artista. Seguono CRAG Home Gallery , con DOMA III – Selected Artworks , e infine Roccatre , dove Ma per le vie del borgo… ricostruisce la memoria artistica di Borgo Nuovo mettendo in dialogo Felice Casorati, Italo Cremona, Francesco Menzio, Giulio Paolini, Giorgio Griffa, Salvo e altri artisti legati alla storia del quartiere.

Il percorso richiede circa 50 minuti di cammino effettivo e, considerando le visite, può occupare all’incirca tre ore.

Da piazza Carlina a San Salvario, fino all’ex Tuxedo

Il secondo nucleo parte da Photo & Contemporary , in via dei Mille 36, con 30 Years of Photo&Contemporary. Lights & Shadows. Part Two . In mostra opere di Georges Rousse, Nils-Udo, Naomi Hatakeyama, Toshio Shibata, Béatrice Helg, Jürgen Klauke e Arno Rafael Minkkinen, accanto a fotografi come Gabriele Basilico, Mimmo Jodice e Luigi Ghirri.

Il percorso prosegue al NH Collection Piazza Carlina , dove TAG esce dagli spazi tradizionali delle gallerie. Qui Mazzoleni presenta special project di Melissa McGill, Marinella Senatore e Massimo Vitali, mentre Photo & Contemporary propone Reinventing the Landscape di Nils-Udo.

Da piazza Carlina si raggiunge A Pick Gallery , con The Gender of Images di Tonino Lacertosa e The Insiders di Sunjing, quest’ultima in collaborazione con Andrea Festa, Roma: due ricerche che affrontano attraverso la pittura questioni legate all’immagine e all’identità.

Ultima tappa è la nuova Galleria Umberto Benappi , negli spazi dell’ex Tuxedo di via Belfiore 8. Join me in the underground riunisce, tra gli altri, Maurizio Camerani, Gianni Dessì, Giuseppe Gallo, Aldo Mondino, Michelangelo Pistoletto, Julian Schnabel e Nunzio, anticipando la vocazione multidisciplinare della nuova sede, pensata per ospitare anche cinema, musica e performance. Durante la TAG Art Night è inoltre prevista Concerto per quattro battiti di Marzio Zorio.

Il cammino complessivo è di circa 25-30 minuti; con le visite, il percorso può essere completato in circa due ore.

Da Vanchiglia ad Aurora e Torino nord

Il terzo itinerario segue invece l’asse che da Vanchiglia porta verso Aurora e la parte settentrionale della città. Si parte da Febo & Dafne , in via Vanchiglia 16, con Invisibile meraviglia. Il disegno nascosto della natura di Massimo Barlettani e Karina Chechik, dedicata alle strutture e alle geometrie latenti del paesaggio naturale.

A poca distanza, Metroquadro presenta Monique Rollins: Solo Exhibition Venice Biennale – Torino , a cura di Roberto Mastroianni, con opere in cui olio, acrilico, carboncino, collage e tessuto costruiscono superfici stratificate tra memoria e tradizione pittorica. Da qui si arriva a Luce Gallery , dove Francesco Pirazzi. Basta giocare trasforma paesaggi e situazioni familiari in immagini sospese, affidate alla pittura e alla luce.

Il percorso prosegue verso CRAG – Chiono Reisova Art Gallery , con Alessandro Cardinale. Slant of Light , nuovo ciclo di sculture nato da una ricerca sulla luce, la percezione e il rapporto tra materia e spazio. Migliaia di superfici lignee dorate cambiano aspetto a seconda dello spostamento dello spettatore.

A chiudere il tragitto è Gagliardi e Domke , in via Cervino 16, con 300km/h . La collettiva riunisce Andrea Di Buduo, Richi Ferrero, Mario Giansone, Glaser/Kunz, Enzo Isaia e Fabio Viale attorno al tema dell’automobile e della velocità, rileggendo uno dei miti fondativi della Torino industriale. Durante la Notte delle Arti Contemporanee Andrea Di Buduo presenterà anche Eterea , automobile interamente customizzata e realizzata a mano come pezzo unico.

Il terzo itinerario richiede circa 45-50 minuti di cammino, cui aggiungere le soste nelle cinque gallerie, per una durata complessiva di circa due ore.

TAG 2026: una mappa aperta della Torino dell’arte

I tre percorsi sono pensati come come nuclei combinabili liberamente nei quattro momenti proposti da TAG durante la settimana di Artissima: la Art Night del 31 ottobre e le tre Art Coffee Breakfast del 30 e 31 ottobre e del 1° novembre. La geografia delle gallerie va così a scandire una mappa aperta della città, da costruire secondo interessi, tempi e quartieri, trasformando i giorni di Artissima anche in un’occasione per attraversare Torino e osservare come il sistema delle gallerie si distribuisce sul territorio e si rinnova, rigorosamente in rete.

title_original: Art Encounters of the Third Kind
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在瑞士的第二周，我往返于温特图尔与苏黎世之间，参加艺术家讲座、参观博物馆，并结识了其他南亚艺术家。

article_text:
My second week in Switzerland was spent getting acquainted with its world-renowned train networks and its clockwork synchronicity. I find myself in an almost hypnotic state, every time I board the train, speeding through green fields by the Toss River, back and forth to Zurich, attending artist talks and visiting museums. While Winterthur has a seasoned, laidback rhythm, blanketed in a calm atmosphere, Zurich feels pulsating with youthful energy and activity. Even the ducks in Lake Zurich wade erratically, trying to keep up with the strong water currents.

I was also lucky enough to befriend two other South Asian artists on residency with Pro Helvetia in Switzerland, Pulak and Madhukar. And soon enough, between the three of us, there was the easy reassurance of free-flowing conversations, an art adda , if you may, as we explored the graffiti at Rote Fabrik, the former factory turned art centre in Zurich.

Communal wall exposing the gritty, rebellious, and urban aesthetic at Rote Fabrik, Zurich

This week, I also welcomed the Bengali new year with a visit to the Black Madonna at Einsiedeln Abbey, a fifteenth-century Benedictine Monastery. As someone who likes to micro-dose on religion from time to time, I have always found faith reassuring, especially when I felt a little unmoored, far away from all the festivities, friends and family.

A view of the Einsiedeln Abbey, housing the Black Madonna in the Chapel of Grace

The highlight of the week, of course, was being invited to Hyderabad-based visual artist Madhukar’s open studio. I was able to get a peek into one of the leading anti-caste voices in experimental artistic practices in the work of at Gleis 70. Leather becomes a tool of resistance in his hands. By crafting it into a thing of beauty, he subverts notions of pollution and purity, and a simple material turns into a complex metaphor.

Installation view of Madhukar Mucharla’s work in his studio at Gleis 70

In contrast to my first week spent in solitude and quiet introspection, the second week brought many conversations, new connections and a host of new inspirations.

title_original: Dana Smessaert: In the Blue Light, I Died
editorial_title_zh: Dana Smessaert: In the Blue Light, I Died

We had lunch together, and honestly, we didn’t separate until two and a half years later, sharing a studio space, duplex, and breakfast on the weekends when we both graduated. As…
